Yehuda Wolf, PA-C
Yehuda joined the Rosh team in 2015 while still a student in PA school. As 
Rapid Review author and editor-in-chief, Yehuda continues to ensure the

from Touro College New York with a Masters in Physician Assistant Studies

Emily Oslie, PA-C
Emily Oslie graduated with a B.S. in applied human biology from Seattle 
Paciﬁ  c University where she played volleyball competitively. After 
graduation, she worked as a medical scribe in emergency departments 
and a primary care oﬃ   ce in Seattle while applying to PA programs. Emily

Adam Rosh, MD
Dr. Adam Rosh is the founder of Rosh Review, which he created in 2011. 
He received his B.A. in biochemistry and M.S. in microbiology from the 
University of Wisconsin, Madison. He received his medical degree from 
Rutgers Medical School and completed his emergency medicine residency 
training at New York University/Bellevue Hospital Center, where he was 
chief resident. Dr. Rosh went on to serve as assistant residency director 
and residency director at Detroit Receiving Hospital. He is the author and 
editor of Pretest Emergency Medicine and Case Files Emergency Medicine 
both published by McGraw Hill. He currently is the CEO of Rosh Review 
and an Attending Emergency Physician.

B. Second-Degree Heart Block (Mobitz I /
Wenckebach) 
Phyysical Exam
• Rhythm will be irregular
Diaggnostic Studies
• ECG with a PR interval that is progressively 
lengthening until QRS complex fails to conduct 
after a P wave ("dropped beat") 
II. Arrhythmias
 • P waves and QRS complexes are normal
 but...
       
• There are dropped beats (P waves without
       QRS complexes)
       
• P-R interval progressively lengthens
       • R-R interval progressively shortens until a
       beat is dropped
       
• Leads to "grouped beating"
       • The block is almost always within the AV
       node

C. Second-Degree Heart Block (Mobitz II) 
Diaggnostic Studies
• ECG with a PR interval that is ﬁxed and 
consistent with “dropped beats”  
Managgement
• Consider permanent pacemaker
Notes
II. Arrhythmias
 • P waves are normal
 • QRS complexes are usually (not always) wide
 due to concomitant bundle branch block
 
• PR intervals are always the same duration
 • There are dropped beats
 • The block is below the AV node, generally in
 the His-Purkinje system

D. Third-Degree Heart Block
Pathopphyysiologgyy
• Associated with aging, anterior or inferior 
infarction, digitalis
Diaggnostic Studies
• ECG with regular P-P and R-R intervals that are 
unrelated to one another 
• Findings represent the independent beating of the 
atria and ventricles 
Managgement
• If symptomatic, treat with atropine, dopamine, or 
temporary pacing
• Deﬁnitive treatment is the placement of a 
permanent pacemaker 
Notes
 • No atrial impulses are conducted 
 • The atria and ventricles beat independently of
 one another
 
• P waves are normal
 • The block can occur at the level of the AV node,
 the bundle of His or the bundle branches
 
• QRS complexes may be narrow (above the
 His bundle) or wide (at or below His bundle)
 depending on the location of the block
 
• No relationship between P waves and QRS
 complexes
 
• Independent and regular atrial rate (constant
 P-P interval)
 
• Slower, independent and constant ventricular
 rate (constant R-R interval)
 • P waves are not related to the QRS complex
 • The PR interval is variable

V. Fetal Distress
A. Components of FHR Evaluation
• Rate (normal = 110–160 bpm):
      • FHR < 110 bpm: bradycardia
      • FHR > 160 bpm: tachycardia
• Variability: 
      • Absent: Indicates severe fetal distress
      • Minimal: < 6 bpm; indicates fetal hypoxia or
      the eﬀ  ects of opioids, magnesium, or sleep
      cycle
      • Normal: 6–25 bpm
      • Marked: > 25 bpm; may indicate fetal
      hypoxia; may occur before a 
decrease in
      variability
      • Sinusoidal: Points to serious fetal anemia; a
      pseudosinusoidal pattern may also occur
      during maternal meperidine use
• Accelerations: Onset of an 
increase in FHR > 15 
beats above baseline to a peak in < 30 seconds. 
Reassuring because they indicate fetal ability to 
appropriately respond to the environment.
• Decelerations: 
      • Early: Visually apparent, gradual (onset to
      nadir in > 30 seconds) 
decrease in FHR with
      a return to baseline that mirrors the uterine
contraction
      • Late: Visually apparent, gradual (onset to
      nadir in > 30 seconds) decrease in FHR with
      return to baseline whose onset, nadir, and
      recovery occur after the beginning, peak, and
      end of uterine contraction, respectively
      • Variable: Abrupt (onset to nadir in < 30
      seconds), visually apparent 
decrease in FHR
      15 bpm below baseline lasting ≥ 15 seconds
      but < 2 minutes
